title: Anacondas: Not Like in the Movie
summary: Josh and Chuck (credited in the transcript as the iHeart Intro speaker) open with banter about the 1997 movie Anaconda and their kids' movie tastes, then do an animal episode on anacondas: size and weight of green, yellow, and dark-spotted anacondas, senses (Jacobson's organ, pit organs), constriction hunting, long fasting and digestion, breeding balls and sexual cannibalism, live birth, and a recent taxonomy revision based on genetic work with a National Geographic project featuring Will Smith. They cover range (including Trinidad), freshwater-only habitat, human encounters (the Paul Rizzuto "Eaten Alive" special, retaliatory vs. preemptive killing, Brazil study), conservation status (least concern), Florida's ban on keeping anacondas as pets, famous captive and wild anacondas (Anna Julia, JLo at the St. Louis Zoo, Oliver at San Francisco Zoo, Annie the tortoise-free record-holding captive snake in Johannesburg). The episode ends with a listener email from Garrett Creeters about his great-great-grandfather Charles Cretors and the popcorn machine.
topics: Will Smith National Geographic anaconda research

segments.title: Anaconda movie banter
segments.summary: Hosts discuss watching the movie Anaconda, its bad-movie reputation, and a kid's reaction to Evil Dead.

segments.title: Anaconda basics and senses
segments.summary: Introduction to anacondas as large boas that are non-venomous and constrict prey; they prefer freshwater swamps and rivers. Discussion of the Jacobson's organ and pit organs for smell and heat detection.

segments.title: Anaconda size, weight, and lifespan
segments.summary: Green anacondas are the heaviest snake, with females much larger than males; yellow anacondas are smaller. Record sizes and weights are discussed, along with lifespan in the wild and captivity.

segments.title: Hunting, digestion, and breeding
segments.summary: Anacondas kill by constriction, cutting blood flow rather than crushing bones; they fast for long periods while digesting. Breeding season, breeding balls, sexual cannibalism, live birth, and litter sizes are covered.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the taxonomy section.

segments.title: Anaconda taxonomy revision
segments.summary: Scientists previously recognized four anaconda species. A recent international study led by Jesus Rivas split green anacondas into two species and merged the other three into one, using genetic analysis. Work included a National Geographic project with Will Smith in Ecuador; genomes of the two green types differ by about 5.5 percent, diverging around ten million years ago.

segments.title: Range and Trinidad
segments.summary: Green anacondas range across South America east of the Andes, as far south as Paraguay, and on Trinidad. The hosts note they are freshwater-only and puzzle over how they reached Trinidad.

segments.title: Break and tangents
segments.summary: Break with off-topic talk about Pee-wee Herman and documentaries before returning to the episode.

segments.title: Eaten Alive and human encounters
segments.summary: Discussion of anacondas attacking humans in rare cases, a Brazilian video of a man bitten free by a snake, and Paul Rizzuto's Discovery Channel special Eaten Alive, which drew criticism and petitions about animal abuse.

segments.title: Human killing of anacondas and conservation
segments.summary: Humans are a bigger threat to anacondas; preemptive killing in communities is common, with a 2015 Brazil study. Discussion of Human Development Index correlation. Anacondas are listed as least concern by the IUCN.

segments.title: Anacondas in Florida and as pets
segments.summary: Anacondas occur in some Florida swamps but are not a major invasive problem; Florida bans them as pets, and they are hard to keep at home.

segments.title: Famous anacondas: Anna Julia, JLo, Oliver, Annie
segments.summary: Anna Julia, a docile 20-foot green anaconda in Brazil's Formoso River, was studied by researchers and died of natural causes weeks after a 2024 paper. JLo lived at the St. Louis Zoo after rescue from a Guyana market. Oliver at San Francisco Zoo may have been the oldest captive anaconda at about 40 years. Annie, a snake at Montecasino Bird Gardens in Johannesburg, is recorded by Guinness at over 37 years old. A mummy voice recreation tangent is included.

segments.title: Listener mail: Cretors popcorn machine
segments.summary: Listener Garrett Cretors writes about his great-great-grandfather Charles Cretors and the popcorn machine, following up on a previous popcorn episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give contact information and the show credits.
